title: Using Adjectives as Nouns
goal: Use Norwegian adjectives as noun phrases with correct definiteness, number, and neuter forms.

objectives.statement: Use Norwegian adjectives as noun phrases with correct definiteness, number, and neuter forms.

spans.value: Maja and Erik are furnishing a small apartment. They have found several possible tables, chairs, lamps, and cupboards, but they cannot take everything.
Hvilket bord skal vi kjøpe?
Det lille passer best på kjøkkenet.

blocks.translation: The small one fits best in the kitchen.

spans.value: Hva med stolene?
Vi tar de blå, ikke de svarte.

blocks.translation: We’ll take the blue ones, not the black ones.

spans.value: Trenger vi også et skap?

blocks.translation: Do we also need a cupboard?

spans.value: Ja, men ikke det høye. Jeg liker det lave.

blocks.translation: Yes, but not the tall one. I like the low one.

spans.value: Og lampene? Den gamle er fin.

blocks.translation: And the lamps? The old one is nice.

spans.value: Den er fin, men vi trenger en ny.

blocks.translation: It is nice, but we need a new one.

spans.value: Maja and Erik repeatedly leave out nouns that are already clear from the conversation. Instead of saying det lille bordet, Erik says det lille. Instead of repeating de blå stolene, he says de blå.

Norwegian can therefore use an adjective as a complete noun phrase. The adjective describes an understood person or thing. Context identifies the omitted noun, while determiners and adjective agreement jointly express relevant features such as number, definiteness, and, in singular forms, gender where the forms distinguish them.
The usual Norwegian term is a nominalized adjective (substantivert adjektiv).

This is similar to English expressions such as the blue one and the old ones. Norwegian does not normally add a word corresponding to one or ones. The adjective takes the agreement form required by the understood noun, although some forms are identical and do not overtly reveal every feature.

sections.title: Understanding what has been left out

spans.value: Look at Erik’s first answer:

The same principle applies to the chairs:
Stolene is definite plural, so the shortened phrase uses de and the plural or definite adjective form blå.
The listener must be able to identify the missing noun from the situation. An adjective cannot normally stand alone if nobody knows what it refers to.

sections.title: Definite forms: the red one and the red ones

spans.value: A definite phrase points to a particular person or thing: the small one, the old one, the blue ones. Norwegian normally uses den, det, or de before a definite adjective used without a noun.

The adjective usually has the definite ending -e in all three patterns.
The understood noun might be en stol, en kopp, or another common-gender noun.
Here the understood noun is neuter, perhaps et skjerf or et glass.
Here more than one item is understood.

statement.value: For a definite adjective phrase without a noun, choose den, det, or de from the gender and number of the understood noun, and normally use the adjective’s -e form.

spans.value: The first sentence in each pair introduces an unspecified item. The second points to a particular item that the speakers can identify.
Another common mistake is to use the English word one as if Norwegian required an extra noun:
This form can occur in informal speech in some contexts, but it is not the basic pattern taught here. The standard, economical phrase is:

sections.title: Plural forms: new ones and the new ones

spans.value: When several items are meant, the adjective takes its plural form. An indefinite plural adjective phrase often has no article:
When the plural group is definite, use de:

en.value: We are buying the new ones.
The cheap ones are by the door.

spans.value: Compare:

en.value: Erik is looking for old lamps.
Erik is looking for old ones.

no.value: Erik ser etter de gamle lampene.

en.value: Erik is looking for the old lamps.
Erik is looking for the old ones.

spans.value: In the indefinite plural, gamle appears without de. In the definite plural, de gamle refers to a particular known group.
Do not automatically use de merely because the meaning is plural. The choice depends on definiteness:
The black items have not yet been identified.
The speakers are choosing a particular visible group.

After walking around the shop, Maja and Erik compare their final choices.
Vi kan ikke kjøpe begge bordene. Tar vi det store eller det lille?

blocks.translation: We can’t buy both tables. Are we taking the large one or the small one?

spans.value: Vi tar det lille. Men vi trenger store stoler.

blocks.translation: We’ll take the small one. But we need large chairs.

spans.value: De store ved vinduet er fine.

blocks.translation: The large ones by the window are nice.

spans.value: Ja, men de er dyre. Finnes det andre stoler?

blocks.translation: Yes, but they are expensive. Are there other chairs?

spans.value: Ja, jeg så noen svarte ved døra.

blocks.translation: Yes, I saw some black ones by the door.

spans.value: Jeg liker ikke de svarte. La oss ta de blå.

blocks.translation: I don’t like the black ones. Let’s take the blue ones.

spans.value: Notice how the same adjective can appear in different phrases as the situation changes:
The items are plural but not yet identified.

no.value: De store ved vinduet er fine.

en.value: The large ones by the window are nice.

spans.value: The speakers now mean a particular group.
Likewise:
This introduces an indefinite group.

en.value: I don’t like the black ones.

spans.value: This refers back to that known group.
The essential decision is not whether the noun is spoken aloud. The essential decision is what the understood noun phrase means:

items.value: If singular, is the understood noun common gender or neuter?
Is the person or thing indefinite or definite?
Which adjective form agrees with those features?

spans.value: At a bakery, Nora and Hassan are choosing
en kake
(a cake) and
et bakverk
(a baked good) for a meeting. Several of each are already on the counter, so both speakers can see which ones they mean.

First describe an unspecified choice, such as wanting a small one or needing two large ones. Then identify a particular visible choice, such as choosing the small one or rejecting the expensive ones. Omit each noun once the context makes it clear.

Without looking back, give Norwegian phrases for an indefinite common-gender one, an indefinite neuter one, a definite common-gender one, a definite neuter one, indefinite plural ones, and definite plural ones, using one familiar adjective.
